summary: The submission benchmarks witness routing policies within a synthetic fault-tolerant memory simulation on an 884,736-cell periodic grid. By evaluating dedicated detector coordinate sampling against shared-line reuse and dense baselines, it demonstrates that dedicated sampling bridges 2.82 retention points over reuse and reaches within 0.20 points of dense selection while sampling under 5.8% of the grid. The study is well controlled with paired confidence intervals, though limited to an idealized synthetic lattice.
strengths: Methodology isolates boundary inference from witness orientation using matched paired seeds and identical baseline conditions.
Comprehensive statistical reporting with 95% paired confidence intervals across multiple rounds and checkpoints.
Exact environment documentation including hardware configuration, OS build, runtime, and specific library versions.
High efficiency trade-off demonstrated, achieving near-dense retention (within 0.20 points) while probing only 5.79% of the detector field.
weaknesses: Evaluated strictly on a synthetic 3D cellular automaton simulation without demonstration on physical or realistic memory hardware architectures.
The grid size is currently fixed at 96³, leaving scalability to larger lattices and varying fault distributions as speculative.
No formal repository was attached to the review interface, limiting automated code pipeline verification.
suggestions: Formally attach the codebase repository to future submissions to qualify for open verification trust badges.
Extend the benchmark across varying grid dimensions (such as the discussed 192³ volume) and different fault densities to evaluate robustness.
Discuss mapping these synthetic detector and witness dynamics to physical memory technologies like RRAM, PCM, or systolic arrays.
